title: Chapter 117: Reason Behind the Hair Washing
html:
Doctor Gao’s message puzzled Chen Ge. “How could washing his hair be a self-defense mechanism?”

“PTSD presupposes an earlier trauma. Men Nan may wash his hair compulsively to escape a painful memory. The answer probably lies in his past.”

“His past?”

“Yes. Something he experienced left him deeply traumatized. Whenever he is reminded of it, his body reacts, and he instinctively seeks relief. From what I’ve observed, washing his hair is how he soothes himself.”

A moment later, another message arrived. “At the beginning of the semester, I asked Men Nan why he had chosen psychology. He said he wanted to cure someone. I realize now that he was probably talking about himself.”

“Then the problem began with something that happened when he was young. We need to ask him for details. We can’t help him without knowing his history.”

“If my diagnosis is correct, that is precisely what we must not do. He has spent years trying to bury the memory. Forcing him to confront it now could push him over the edge.”

“Then we can ask his family. He’s suffering this badly, yet his parents show no concern? Something isn’t right.” Chen Ge was tempted to photograph Men Nan and send the picture to them.

“I questioned them when I called earlier. Men Nan has washed his hair obsessively since childhood. His parents are so accustomed to it that they no longer consider it a problem.”

“Did they say why this happened?”

“No. His parents did take him to a psychiatrist when he was small. The diagnosis was OCD, which was unusual in a child his age. Because he was too young for medication, the psychiatrist advised his parents to stay close and give him constant support.”

“They clearly ignored that advice,” Chen Ge replied at once. Parents who cared about their son would not behave so coldly.

“His symptoms were mild enough not to disrupt his daily life, so they dismissed them. I also learned that Men Nan’s biological mother died when he was five or six. His father later remarried and had another son.”

“His biological mother died?” At last, the investigation had found a lead.

“His biological parents had a poor relationship. His father was rarely home, so his mother raised him almost alone. Then one day, a burglar broke into the house. Men Nan’s current family doesn’t know exactly what followed. They only know that a neighbor called the police the next morning.”

“The next day?” Chen Ge’s heart skipped a beat. “Then, where was Men Nan during the time of the crime?”

“I’m not sure, but according to the neighbor, Men Nan was already at the scene when the police arrived. He was the one who found his mother.”

A chill crept up Chen Ge’s spine as he read the message. “You mean Men Nan spent the night in the house with his mother’s body and wasn’t discovered until morning?”

“That appears to be what happened. Perhaps the burglar took pity on him, or perhaps Men Nan was asleep during the crime. Either way, he survived, but finding his mother dead must have scarred him deeply. I suspect both his OCD and PTSD stem from the murder. What I don’t understand is the hair washing. How is that connected?”

Doctor Gao was as confused as Chen Ge. Standing before the mirror, Chen Ge studied his reflection. Washing his hair as self-defense?

He pictured himself bent over the sink, then touched the back of his neck as realization struck. That drop of water!

He immediately messaged Doctor Gao. “At the crime scene, where was the body of Men Nan’s mother discovered?”

“After killing her, the burglar removed the moisture-resistant panels above the bathroom ceiling and hid her body there. The crime might have gone undiscovered much longer if the neighbor’s child hadn’t attended school with Men Nan. The two families knew each other well, so the neighbor realized something was wrong.”

“Above the bathroom?” Chen Ge looked up. The low ceiling seemed to press down on him. “I think I understand why Men Nan compulsively washes his hair.”

He typed a reply. “Could this be what happened? Men Nan and his mother discovered the burglar. She told him to hide while she called the police, but the burglar caught her.”

“That’s possible, but what does that have to do with hair washing?”

“Men Nan witnessed the murder, then hid until the burglar left. When he went looking for his mother, her blood dripped onto his head from the bathroom ceiling.” Typing the words made Chen Ge’s stomach turn. “Now, whenever liquid touches his head or something recalls that night, he washes his hair over and over, trying to wash the memory away. You were right, Doctor Gao—this is more than simple OCD.”

After sending the message, Chen Ge looked out of the bathroom. Shock covered Doctor Gao’s face. Their eyes met.

“We’ve found the cause!” Doctor Gao put away his phone and approached him. “I’ll take him away and begin treatment for the trauma.”

“I’m afraid it isn’t that simple.” Chen Ge glanced at Men Nan and shook his head. “The hair washing itself never frightened him. The true horror in his dream is the man drawing closer. If we want to help Men Nan, we have to identify that man and drive him out of the dream.”

“Drive something out of his dream?” Doctor Gao regarded Chen Ge suspiciously, then looked at Men Nan’s unnatural posture. For a moment, he felt as though he were back in the psychiatric hospital. “Are you joking?”

“I have a theory. Tonight will prove whether I’m right.” After connecting the clues, Chen Ge was about sixty percent confident. “There really are three ‘people’ in this room. We’ve identified two of them. Now we only need to solve the mystery of the third.”
